A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SynCD research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised, relocated, and added material.

before.justification: V1 reports original DreamBooth and CustomConcept101 experiments, model and dataset ablations, and human preference studies in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds FLUX customization results, baseline comparisons, and training-data analyses, including an OminiControl human preference comparison.

M1.justification: V2 adds a 12B FLUX customization model alongside the retained U-Net variants. It uses flow prediction and clean reference features without IP-Adapter initialization or foreground masking, unlike the noisy, masked U-Net conditioning path (Section 4; Appendix C.2). The rigid-data generator also changes from XLabs depth ControlNet to FLUX-Depth.

E1.justification: DreamBooth, CustomConcept101, and SynCD's rigid/deformable object coverage remain. V2 additionally trains on OminiControl's paired synthetic images for a controlled dataset comparison (Appendix B, Table 9), extending training-data coverage within the existing customization task.

E2.justification: V2 adds OminiControl and FLUX IP-Adapter to benchmark comparisons and FLUX LoRA to optimization-based comparisons. Its human study adds Ours (12B) versus OminiControl but drops v1's single-input Ours (1B) versus JeDi and three-input Ours (3B) versus JeDi comparisons. Most earlier benchmark comparators remain.

E3.justification: Appendix C changes the reported U-Net learning rate from 1e-5 to 5e-6 and replaces fixed two-reference training with horizontal-flip augmentation by variable one- or two-reference training. Rigid-data generation changes from 50 to 30 sampling steps with revised guidance settings. V2 also introduces FLUX training and inference protocols and drops the filtering-rate metric. These reported changes do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds controlled SynCD-versus-OminiControl training, FLUX dataset-size sensitivity, model-dependent viewpoint comparisons, and low-aesthetic-data and reference-pose failure analyses. It removes the explicit mask/global-feature ablations from v1 Table 4 and the dataset-size human preference study from v1 Appendix B. Existing category-diversity and guidance analyses are substantially retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that human preference standard errors are within +/-5% (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 2). V2 adds no seed reporting, repeated-run counts, confidence-interval procedure, or significance testing; additional comparison rows retain the existing uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds FLUX benchmark and ablation results, including 58.02% overall human preference over OminiControl. Under revised generation settings, rigid-object ablation scores change from 0.595/0.591/0.534 to 0.598/0.572/0.495 (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 4). Filtering rates and several human-study results disappear. Most retained U-Net and CustomConcept101 scores remain unchanged, while new FLUX entries disagree across v2 Tables 1, 7, and 9.

T1.justification: Section 4 extends the formal training objective to flow prediction, defining its target as epsilon minus x alongside diffusion velocity prediction (Equation 3). The shared-attention and normalized-guidance formulations remain substantively equivalent. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: consistent multi-image synthetic data, shared-attention reference conditioning, and normalized guidance for improved customization. The claims of outperforming encoder-based baselines and competing with optimization-based approaches remain; the FLUX experiments broaden their supporting evidence.

C2.justification: V2 interprets lower FLUX similarity scores through greater viewpoint/background diversity, warns that automatic metrics can favor copying reference objects, and qualifies dataset-size benefits by model architecture. Section 6 and Appendix D add single-object scope, reference-pose-dependent failures, and explanations of synthetic-data artifacts, replacing v1's detailed-texture limitation focus. Warping is now interpreted as improving quantitative consistency as well as visual consistency.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds LoRA ranks, FLUX optimizer and sampling details, explicit camera-viewpoint sampling, runtimes separated by reference count, and guidance-rescale implementation details. Conversely, v1's zero-SNR schedule, 10% auxiliary image-text training, and 5% condition-dropout disclosures are absent; their actual removal from training is not established. The project code/data link is unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 positions OminiControl as concurrent synthetic-data work and adds references for flow matching, Prodigy, FLUX components, and synthetic-data collapse. It removes the general image-conditioned-generation paragraph and associated citations, including GLIGEN and Context Diffusion. The central positioning around shared attention and explicit 3D consistency constraints remains.

P1.justification: V2 substantially restructures the method and experimental narrative: three method subsections become a unified Section 4, training details move into experiments, qualitative comparisons precede quantitative ones, and optimization-based comparisons move to Appendix A. Filtering receives its own subsection, and the introduction, ablation discussion, and limitations are extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview and training diagrams, reorganizes qualitative grids around FLUX, merges optimization-comparison figures, and adds dataset-comparison and failure-analysis displays. Main comparison and ablation tables are substantially restructured; input-count group labels disappear from the main benchmark and human-study tables. Several unchanged appendix figures are merely renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens the paper with FLUX transfer experiments, a controlled alternative-training-data comparison, concrete data-quality analyses, and fuller implementation details. These gains are tempered by removed component ablations and unexplained FLUX score inconsistencies: the three-input GeometricScore is 0.780 in Tables 1 and 9 but 0.765 in Table 7. The added evidence supports a limited overall improvement.
